ja: だいにじゅうろくかい

p.src: After thirty-three days of convalescence, Baoyu had not only recovered his strength, but even the sores on his face had healed smooth, and he returned to the Prospect Garden. There is no need to dwell on that. During Baoyu’s recent illness, Jia Yun had brought household servants to keep watch at night and had remained there day and night. Hongyu and the other maids had also stayed there to attend Baoyu, and after seeing one another for so many days, they had gradually become familiar. When Hongyu saw the handkerchief in Jia Yun’s hand, it looked very much like the one she had lost before. She wanted to ask him about it, but could not bring herself to do so. Unexpectedly, after the monk and the Taoist had come, there was no further need for any of the men, and Jia Yun went back to planting trees. She tried to put the matter aside, yet could not let it go; she wanted to ask him, yet feared arousing suspicion. Just as she wavered in indecision, her mind in turmoil, she suddenly heard someone outside the window ask, “Sister, are you in?” Hearing this, Hongyu peered through the window and saw that it was a young maid from their own courtyard named Jiahui. She answered, “I’m here. Come in.” Jiahui ran in at once, sat down on the bed, and said with a laugh, “What good luck I’ve had! I was washing things in the courtyard just now when Baoyu asked that some tea be sent to Miss Lin, and Sister Hua gave it to me to deliver. As luck would have it, the Old Lady had just sent money to Miss Lin, and they were dividing it among her maids. When Miss Lin saw me, she scooped up two handfuls for me. I don’t even know how much there is. Keep it safe for me.” She opened her handkerchief and poured out the coins, and Hongyu carefully counted every one before putting them away for her.

p.src: Jiahui asked, “How have you really been feeling lately? If you ask me, you ought to go home for a couple of days, have a doctor examine you, and take a few doses of medicine. Then you’ll be well.” Hongyu replied, “What are you talking about? There’s nothing wrong with me. Why should I go home?” Jiahui said, “I’ve just thought of something. Miss Lin is frail and often takes medicine. You could ask her for some and take that—it would do just as well.” Hongyu said, “Nonsense! Medicine isn’t something you can take at random.” Jiahui said, “But you can’t go on like this, with no appetite for food or drink. What will become of you in the end?” Hongyu replied, “What is there to fear? I’d be better off dying sooner and having done with it!” Jiahui said, “Why say such things when there’s nothing the matter?” Hongyu said, “What do you know of what weighs on my heart?”

Hongyu said, “What do you know of what weighs on my heart?”

p.src: Jiahui nodded and thought for a while before saying, “I can hardly blame you. It’s difficult to find one’s footing in this place. Only yesterday, because Baoyu had been ill for so many days, the Old Lady said that everyone who had attended him had worked hard. Now that he had recovered and the vows made at all the shrines had been fulfilled, she ordered that all who had waited on him be rewarded according to rank. We are young and don’t rank high enough, so I have no complaint—but how could even you be left out? That is something I cannot accept. Even if Xiren received the fullest possible share, I wouldn’t resent her; she deserves it. In all honesty, who would dare compare herself with her? Quite apart from how attentive and careful she always is, even if she were not, no one could rival her standing. What is infuriating is that Qingwen, Qixia, and the others were all placed in the highest rank. They rely on their parents’ influence, and everyone goes out of their way to flatter them. Tell me, isn’t that maddening?” Hongyu said, “There’s no point in being angry with them. As the saying goes, ‘Though a thousand-mile awning may be raised, there is no banquet that does not end.’ Who stays with anyone for a lifetime? In another three or five years, each of us will have gone off to her own affairs. By then, who will concern herself with anyone else?” These few words touched Jiahui’s heart, and despite herself her eyes reddened. Too embarrassed to burst into tears for no apparent reason, she forced a smile and said, “What you say is true. Only yesterday Baoyu was still talking about how he would arrange the rooms and have clothes made in the days to come, as though there were hundreds of years ahead of us to endure.”

p.src: Hongyu gave two cold laughs and was just about to speak when a little maid whose hair had not yet been put up came in, carrying some embroidery patterns and two sheets of paper. “Here are two designs they want you to copy,” she said. With that, she tossed them down before Hongyu, turned, and ran away. Hongyu called after her, “Whose are they, anyway? You run off without even waiting for me to finish! Is someone keeping steamed buns hot for you, afraid they might grow cold?” From outside the window, the little maid called back only, “They belong to big sister Qi.” Then off she went again, her feet thumping on the ground. In a temper, Hongyu flung the patterns aside and searched a drawer for a brush. After rummaging for a long time, she found that every one was worn down. “Where did I put that new brush I had the other day? Why can’t I remember all of a sudden?” As she spoke, she fell into thought. After pondering for a while, she smiled. “Of course! Ying’er took it the other evening.” Then she said to Jiahui, “Go and fetch it for me.” “Big sister Hua is waiting for me to help her carry a chest,” said Jiahui. “Go and get it yourself.” “If she’s waiting for you,” said Hongyu, “why are you still sitting here idly chattering? If I hadn’t asked you to fetch it, she wouldn’t be waiting for you at all. You thoroughly wicked little minx!” So saying, she left the room herself, went out of Happy Red Court, and headed straight for Baochai’s residence. Just as she reached the side of Qinfang Pavilion, she saw Baoyu’s former wet nurse, Nanny Li, approaching from the other direction. Hongyu stopped and asked with a smile, “Nanny Li, where have you been? What brings you this way?” Nanny Li stopped and slapped her hand against her thigh. “Just listen to this! For no good reason, he has taken a fancy to some young fellow who plants trees—Yun or Yu or whatever his name is—and now he has forced me to summon him here. If the senior ladies hear of it tomorrow, there will be trouble again.” Hongyu laughed. “Did you really indulge him and go summon the fellow?” “What else could I do?” replied Nanny Li. Hongyu smiled. “If that fellow has any sense of propriety, he ought to decline to come in.” “He isn’t a fool,” said Nanny Li. “Why wouldn’t he come in?” “If he is coming in,” said Hongyu, “you ought to return with him. It would hardly do to let him blunder about alone when he arrives.” “Do you think I have time to walk with him?” said Nanny Li. “I merely told him what to do. When he arrives, we can send a little maid or an old serving woman to bring him in, and that will be the end of it.” With that, she went straight on her way, leaning on her cane. On hearing this, Hongyu stood lost in thought and for the moment forgot all about fetching the brush.

p.src: Presently a little maid came running up. Seeing Hongyu standing there, she asked, “Sister Lin, what are you doing here?” Hongyu looked up and saw that it was the little maid Zhui’er. “Where are you going?” Hongyu asked. “They told me to bring Second Master Yun inside,” replied Zhui’er. With that, she ran straight on. Hongyu had just reached the gate by Wasp-Waist Bridge when she saw Zhui’er approaching from the other side with Jia Yun. As Jia Yun walked along, he stole a sidelong glance at Hongyu. Pretending merely to be speaking with Zhui’er, Hongyu likewise glanced at Jia Yun. The moment their eyes met, Hongyu involuntarily blushed, turned sharply away, and went toward All-Spice Court. But no more of this for now.

p.src: Meanwhile, Jia Yun followed Zhui’er along the winding way until they reached Happy Red Court. Zhui’er went in first to announce him and only then led Jia Yun inside. Looking around, Jia Yun saw several artfully placed rocks in the courtyard and plantains growing among them; farther off, two cranes preened their feathers beneath the pines. Along the covered gallery hung cages of every kind, housing all manner of rare and marvelous birds. Ahead stood a modest five-bay portico, its matching partitions carved throughout with fresh and intricate designs. Above it hung a tablet inscribed in four large characters: “Happy Red and Delightful Green.” Jia Yun thought, “No wonder it is called Happy Red Court; so those are the four words on its tablet.” While he was thinking this, he heard a laughing voice from within, beyond a gauze-covered window: “Do come in! How could I have forgotten you for two or three whole months!” Recognizing Baoyu’s voice, Jia Yun hurried into the room. He looked up and saw gold and jade gleaming everywhere and richly patterned decorations flashing in the light, yet Baoyu himself was nowhere to be seen. Turning his head, he saw a large full-length mirror standing on the left. From behind it emerged two maids of about fifteen or sixteen, both of the same height. “Please come and sit in the inner room, Second Master,” they said. Jia Yun did not even dare look directly at them and hastily assented. Passing through another green gauze partition, he saw a small lacquered bed hung with bright-red curtains patterned with scattered flowers in gold. Baoyu, dressed in informal clothes with his shoes slipped loosely on, was reclining on the bed with a book in his hand. Seeing Jia Yun enter, he tossed the book aside and rose at once, his face wreathed in smiles. Jia Yun hurried forward and paid his respects. Baoyu invited him to sit, and Jia Yun took a chair below him. Baoyu smiled. “When I saw you that month, I told you to come and visit me in my study. But one thing after another kept happening, and somehow I forgot all about you.” Jia Yun smiled. “It was simply my bad luck that Uncle happened to be unwell. Are you fully recovered now, Uncle?” “Quite recovered,” said Baoyu. “I heard that you worked very hard for several days on my account.” “It was only right that I should,” replied Jia Yun. “Your recovery, Uncle, is a blessing to our whole family.”

p.src: As he spoke, a maid came in carrying tea for him. Jia Yun went on talking with Baoyu, but his eyes stole toward the maid: she was slender and tall, with a longish face, and wore a silvery-red jacket, a blue satin vest, and a finely pleated white silk skirt. She was none other than Xiren. When Baoyu had been ill for several days, Jia Yun had spent two days mingling with the people inside and had learned to recognize about half of the better-known members of the household. He also knew that Xiren held a special place among the maids in Baoyu’s rooms. Seeing her bring the tea while Baoyu sat nearby, he hurriedly rose and said with a smile, “Why should you pour tea for me, elder sister? I’ve come to my uncle’s quarters, so I’m hardly a guest. Please let me pour it myself.” “Just stay seated,” said Baoyu. There’s no need for ceremony before the maids.” Jia Yun smiled. “Even so, how could I presume before the elder sisters in your rooms, Uncle?” As he spoke, he sat down and drank his tea.

p.src: Baoyu then chatted with him about one inconsequential thing after another. He spoke of whose actors were best and whose garden finest; he told him whose maid was prettiest, whose banquets most lavish, and which household possessed some rare treasure or other curiosity. Jia Yun could only humor him. After they had talked awhile, he noticed that Baoyu was growing listless, so he rose to take his leave. Baoyu made little effort to detain him and merely said, “Come again tomorrow if you’re free.” He again ordered the young maid Zhuier to see him out.

p.src: Once outside Happy Red Court, Jia Yun saw that no one was about. He slowed his steps and began asking Zhuier one question after another: “How old are you? What is your name? What work do your parents do? How many years have you served in Uncle Bao’s rooms? How much are you paid each month? Altogether, how many girls serve in Uncle Bao’s rooms?” At his questions, Zhuier told him everything item by item. Jia Yun then asked, “Was that girl who spoke to you just now called Xiaohong?” Zhuier laughed. “Yes, she is called Xiaohong. Why do you ask about her?” “Just now,” said Jia Yun, “she asked you about a handkerchief. As it happens, I found one.” Hearing this, Zhuier laughed. “She has asked me several times whether I had seen her handkerchief. As if I had that much time to spare on such things! She asked me again today and said that if I found it for her, she would thank me. She said it at the entrance to Allspice Court just now; you heard it yourself, Second Master, so you know I’m not lying. Dear Second Master, since you found it, please give it to me. I want to see how she will thank me.” It turned out that when Jia Yun had come into the garden to plant trees the previous month, he had found a gauze-silk handkerchief. He knew it must have been lost by someone living in the garden, but since he did not know whose it was, he had not dared act rashly. Now, hearing Hongyu ask Zhuier about it, he knew that it belonged to Hongyu, and his heart overflowed with delighted good fortune. When Zhuier pressed him for it, he already had a plan. He drew one of his own handkerchiefs from his sleeve and said to her with a smile, “I’ll give it to you, but if she rewards you, you mustn’t keep it secret from me.” Zhuier readily promised, took the handkerchief, saw Jia Yun out, and returned to look for Hongyu. We need say no more of that for now.

p.src: Now let us return to Baoyu. After seeing Jia Yun off, he lay listlessly askew on the bed, seemingly on the verge of drifting into sleep. Xiren came over, sat on the edge of the bed, and nudged him. “Why are you going to sleep again? You’re terribly bored. Why not go outside for a stroll?” At this, Baoyu took her hand and said with a smile, “I would go, but I can’t bear to leave you.” “Come, get up!” Xiren said with a laugh. As she spoke, she pulled Baoyu to his feet. “But where am I to go?” asked Baoyu. Everything feels so wearisome and vexing.” “You’ll feel better once you’re outside,” said Xiren. If you go on languishing here like this, you’ll only feel more vexed and weary.”

p.src: Baoyu was dispirited, but he had no choice except to do as she said. He sauntered from the room, teased the birds awhile in the covered gallery, then went beyond the courtyard and watched the goldfish for a time along the Qinfang Stream. Presently he saw two young deer come racing down the hillside like arrows, though he could not imagine why. While he was still wondering, Jia Lan came running after them with a little bow in his hand. Seeing Baoyu ahead, he stopped and said with a smile, “So Second Uncle is at home! I thought you had gone out.” “You’re up to mischief again,” said Baoyu. Why shoot at the poor creatures when they’ve done nothing?” Jia Lan laughed. “I’m not studying just now, so what else should I do with my free time? That is why I’m practicing riding and archery.” “You won’t practice anymore once you’ve fallen and knocked your teeth out,” said Baoyu.

Jia Lan laughed. “I’m not studying just now, so what else should I do with my free time?
That is why I’m practicing riding and archery.”
“You won’t practice anymore once you’ve fallen and knocked your teeth out,” said Baoyu.

p.src: With that, Baoyu wandered on wherever his feet took him until he reached the gate of a courtyard, where phoenix-tail bamboos stood in dense ranks and murmured faintly like dragons. Looking up at the gate, he saw the three characters “Xiaoxiang Lodge” inscribed on its plaque. Baoyu strolled inside. Bamboo blinds hung to the floor, and not a voice could be heard. Approaching the window, he caught a thread of subtle fragrance stealing through its green gauze. Baoyu pressed his face to the gauze and peered inside. Suddenly he heard a soft, lingering sigh: “‘Each day, beset by yearning, I languish into drowsiness.’” At these words, an irresistible tingling stirred in Baoyu’s heart. Looking again, he saw Daiyu stretching herself on the bed. From outside the window Baoyu laughed and asked, “Why are you ‘each day beset by yearning, languishing into drowsiness’?” As he spoke, he lifted the curtain and entered.

p.src: Realizing that she had unwittingly betrayed her feelings, Lin Daiyu blushed, covered her face with her sleeve, turned toward the inside of the bed, and pretended to be asleep. Baoyu had just come forward to turn her around when Daiyu’s nurse and two elderly maids followed him in and said, “Your cousin is asleep. Please come again when she wakes.” No sooner had they spoken than Daiyu turned over and sat up, saying with a smile, “Who is asleep?” Seeing Daiyu rise, the two or three women laughed. “We thought you were asleep, miss.” Then they called to Zijuan, “Miss is awake. Come in and attend her.” With that, they all went away.

p.src: Daiyu sat up on the bed, raising a hand to tidy the hair at her temples as she smiled at Baoyu. “Why did you come in while I was asleep?” Seeing her starry eyes still heavy with sleep and her fragrant cheeks flushed, Baoyu felt his soul take flight. He dropped sideways into a chair and asked with a smile, “What did you just say?” “I didn’t say anything,” replied Daiyu. Baoyu laughed. “Here’s a knuckle-rap for you! I heard every word.”

p.src: While the two were talking, Zijuan came in. Baoyu said with a smile, “Zijuan, pour me a bowl of your good tea.” “What good tea have we got?” said Zijuan. If you want anything good, you must wait until Xiren comes.” “Pay no attention to him,” said Daiyu. “Go and draw some water for me first.” Zijuan smiled. “He is our guest, so naturally I must serve him tea before I fetch your water.” With that, she went to pour the tea. Baoyu laughed. “What a good girl! ‘If you shared the lovebird’s bed with your tender young mistress, how could you bear to fold the quilts and make the bed?’” Lin Daiyu’s face instantly darkened. “Second Brother,” she said, “what did you just say?” Baoyu smiled. “I didn’t say anything.” Daiyu burst into tears. “So this is the latest fashion: you hear vulgar talk outside and repeat it to me; you read filthy books and then use them to make fun of me. I have become nothing but a plaything for young gentlemen to amuse themselves with.” Still weeping, she climbed down from the bed and made for the door. Baoyu did not know what she meant to do. Alarmed, he hurried after her. “Dear sister, I deserve to die for speaking so thoughtlessly. Please don’t go and tell anyone. If I ever dare do it again, may a boil grow on my mouth and my tongue rot away.” As he spoke, Xiren came over and said, “Hurry back and get dressed. Master wants to see you.” The news struck Baoyu like a thunderclap. Forgetting everything else, he rushed back to dress. When he came out of the garden, he found Beiming waiting by the inner gate. Baoyu asked, “Do you know why I have been summoned?” “Please hurry out, young master,” said Beiming. “You must go and see him anyway, and you’ll find out when you get there.” As he spoke, he kept urging Baoyu onward.

p.src: Even after they had passed the great hall, Baoyu was still full of misgivings. Suddenly a peal of laughter came from beside the wall. Turning, he saw Xue Pan emerge, clapping his hands and laughing. “If I hadn’t said your uncle wanted you, how could I ever have got you out so quickly?” Beiming laughed too. “Please don’t blame me, young master.” He hastily dropped to his knees. Baoyu stood stunned for some time before realizing that Xue Pan had tricked him into coming out. Xue Pan hastily bowed again and again in apology, pleading, “Don’t make things hard for the boy. I forced him to do it.” There was nothing Baoyu could do. He could only smile and ask, “Even if you meant to trick me, why did you have to bring my father into it? I shall tell Aunt about this and ask her to judge whether you were right to do such a thing.” “Dear brother,” Xue Pan hastily replied, “I was so anxious to get you out quickly that I forgot how unlucky it was to say such a thing. Another day, you may trick me in the same way and say it is my father; then we shall be even.” “Oh, stop!” said Baoyu. “That only makes it worse.” Then he turned to Beiming. “You mutinous little bastard, what are you still kneeling there for?” Beiming hurriedly kowtowed and rose. Xue Pan said, “I would not have dared disturb you if it were not for this. Tomorrow, the third day of the fifth month, is my birthday. Cheng Rixing, the antique dealer, somehow managed to find a fresh lotus root this thick and long, white and crisp; an enormous watermelon; a fresh sturgeon this long; and a Siamese pig this big, tribute from the Kingdom of Siam and smoked with fragrant sacred cypress. Tell me, are those four gifts rare or not? The fish and the pig are merely costly and hard to obtain, but how he managed to grow that lotus root and melon is beyond me. I promptly presented some to my mother, then hurried to send portions to your grandmother, uncle, and aunt. I still have some left. I feared that eating it all myself might diminish my store of blessings, and after much thought I decided that, apart from me, you alone were worthy of eating it. That is why I especially invited you here. As luck would have it, the young singers have just arrived too. What do you say to our making merry together all day?” As he spoke, they arrived at his study. Zhan Guang, Cheng Rixing, Hu Silai, Shan Pingren, and the singers were all there. When Baoyu entered, some paid their respects and others exchanged greetings, until everyone had been introduced. After they had taken tea, Xue Pan ordered the servants to bring in the wine. Before he had finished speaking, the pages all set to work at once; after bustling about for quite some time, they finally had everything ready and the guests took their seats. Baoyu saw that the melon and lotus root were indeed remarkable. He smiled and said, “I have not even sent you my birthday present yet, but here I am already imposing on your hospitality.” “Quite so,” said Xue Pan. “What will you give me tomorrow?” “What could I possibly have to give you?” said Baoyu.

p.src: As for money, food, or clothing, none of those things truly belongs to me. Only a piece of calligraphy I write or a picture I paint can really be called mine.”

u.src: As for money, food, or clothing, none of those things truly belongs to me. Only a piece of calligraphy I write or a picture I paint can really be called mine.”

p.src: Xue Pan laughed. “Now that you mention paintings, I’ve just remembered something. Yesterday I saw an erotic painting at someone’s house, and it was remarkably well done. There was a great deal of writing on it too, though I didn’t look closely. I only saw the signature—it was painted by ‘Geng Huang.’ It was truly superb beyond words!” Hearing this, Baoyu wondered to himself, “I have seen my share of calligraphy and paintings, ancient and modern, but whoever heard of a ‘Geng Huang’?” After pondering for quite a while, he suddenly burst out laughing. He had someone bring a brush, wrote two characters on his palm, and asked Xue Pan, “Are you certain you saw ‘Geng Huang’?” “How could I have seen it wrong?” said Xue Pan. Baoyu opened his hand and showed it to him. “Could it have been these two characters? They are not so very different from ‘Geng Huang,’ after all.” Everyone looked and saw that the characters were in fact “Tang Yin.” They all laughed. “Those must have been the two. Perhaps Your Lordship’s eyes blurred for a moment.” Xue Pan felt rather foolish and laughed. “How was I to know whether it was ‘Tang Yin’ or ‘fruit silver’?” As they were speaking, a page came in to announce, “Master Feng has arrived.” Baoyu knew at once that the visitor was Feng Ziying, son of Feng Tang, the Divine-Might General. Xue Pan and the others all cried together, “Invite him in at once!” Before they had finished speaking, Feng Ziying came in, talking and laughing all the way. Everyone hurriedly rose from the table and offered him a seat. Feng Ziying laughed. “Well, well! So you no longer go out, but stay home enjoying yourselves instead.” Baoyu and Xue Pan both laughed. “We haven’t seen you for some time. Is your venerable father in good health?” Ziying replied, “Thanks to your good wishes, my father is quite well. My mother, however, recently caught a slight chill and was unwell for a couple of days.” Noticing some bruising on his face, Xue Pan laughed. “Who have you been trading punches with this time? You’re wearing the signboard for all to see.” Feng Ziying laughed. “Ever since I injured Commandant Qiu’s son in that fight, I have resolved never to lose my temper again. How could I have been trading punches? This mark on my face came the other day while we were hunting at Iron-Net Mountain—a falcon’s wing caught me a glancing blow.” “When was that?” asked Baoyu. “We left on the twenty-eighth of the third month,” said Ziying, “and returned just the day before yesterday.” “No wonder I didn’t see you on the third or fourth the other day, when I attended a banquet at Cousin Shen’s house,” said Baoyu. I meant to ask about you, but somehow it slipped my mind. Did you go alone, or did your venerable father go as well?” Ziying replied, “It was precisely because my father was going that I had no choice but to accompany him. Do you think I had gone mad from idleness? Why abandon the pleasure of drinking and listening to songs with all of you to seek out such hardship? Yet this time, amid great misfortune, there was also great good fortune.”

p.src: When Xue Pan and the others saw that he had finished his tea, they all said, “Come and take your place at the table. You can tell us the story at leisure.” At this, Feng Ziying stood and said, “By rights I ought to stay and drink a few cups with you, but today I have a matter of the utmost importance and must return to report it to my father in person, so I truly dare not accept.” But Xue Pan, Baoyu, and the rest would not hear of it and clung to him, refusing to let him go. Feng Ziying laughed. “This is strange indeed. In all the years we have known one another, when have we ever stood on such ceremony? I truly cannot oblige you today. If you insist that I drink, bring me a large cup, and I shall take two cups—that is all.” Hearing this, the others had no choice but to relent. Xue Pan took up the winepot and Baoyu held the cup, and together they poured him two enormous bowlfuls. Feng Ziying remained standing and drained them both in a single breath. Baoyu said, “Before you leave, you must at least finish telling us about this ‘good fortune amid misfortune.’” Feng Ziying laughed. “There would not be time to tell it properly today. On account of this very matter, I intend to give a special dinner and invite you all to discuss it in detail; besides, I have a favor to ask of you.” With that, he clasped their hands in farewell and made to leave. Xue Pan said, “You have only made us more eager, and now we cannot let the matter go. Tell us when you mean to invite us. Then at least we need not be kept in suspense.” Feng Ziying replied, “Ten days at most, eight at the least.” Still speaking, he went out, mounted his horse, and rode away. The others returned to their places, drank for a while longer, and then dispersed.

p.src: As it happened, Qingwen and Bihen had just quarreled and Qingwen was in a foul temper. When Baochai arrived, Qingwen vented her anger on her and grumbled in the courtyard, “She comes and sits here whether she has any business or not, keeping us from sleeping until the middle of the night!” Just then someone else called at the gate. Qingwen grew angrier still and, without even asking who it was, said, “Everyone is in bed. Come back tomorrow!” Daiyu knew the maids’ ways well. They were accustomed to joking and playing tricks on one another, so she supposed that the girls inside had not recognized her voice and had mistaken her for another maid, which was why they would not open the gate. She therefore called more loudly, “It is I. Won’t you open the gate?” But Qingwen still failed to recognize her voice and snapped willfully, “I don’t care who you are. Master Bao has ordered that no one at all is to be let in!” Hearing this, Daiyu stood frozen with anger outside the gate. She was about to demand an explanation in a loud voice and start a quarrel, but then she reconsidered: “Although my aunt’s home is said to be as good as my own, I am still a guest here after all. Now that both my parents are dead and I have no one to depend upon, I am living under their roof. If I truly make a scene now, I shall only make myself ridiculous.” As she thought this, tears rolled down her cheeks once more. She could neither bring herself to leave nor remain standing there. While she stood there at a loss, she heard a burst of laughter and conversation from within. Listening closely, she realized that the voices belonged to Baoyu and Baochai. Daiyu grew angrier than ever. Turning it over and over in her mind, she suddenly remembered what had happened that morning: “Baoyu must be angry because I threatened to tell on him. But when did I ever tell on you? You could at least have asked before becoming so angry with me that you treat me like this. You refuse to let me in today, but do you imagine we shall never meet again tomorrow?” The more she thought, the more heartsick she became. Heedless of the cold dew on the moss and the chill wind along the flower path, she stood alone beneath the blossoms by a corner of the wall and began to sob in bitter sorrow. Daiyu possessed beauty unrivaled in her age and a grace rarely seen in the world. No sooner did she begin to weep than the roosting birds and crows among the nearby willow branches and blossoms, hearing her cries, all fluttered up and fled far away, unable to bear listening any longer. Truly:

Daiyu knew the maids’ ways well. They were accustomed to joking and playing tricks on one another, so she supposed that the girls inside had not recognized her voice and had mistaken her for another maid, which was why they would not open the gate. She therefore called more loudly, “It is I. Won’t you open the gate?”
But Qingwen still failed to recognize her voice and snapped willfully, “I don’t care who you are. Master Bao has ordered that no one at all is to be let in!”

Hearing this, Daiyu stood frozen with anger outside the gate. She was about to demand an explanation in a loud voice and start a quarrel, but then she reconsidered: “Although my aunt’s home is said to be as good as my own, I am still a guest here after all.
Now that both my parents are dead and I have no one to depend upon, I am living under their roof.
If I truly make a scene now, I shall only make myself ridiculous.”
As she thought this, tears rolled down her cheeks once more.
She could neither bring herself to leave nor remain standing there.
While she stood there at a loss, she heard a burst of laughter and conversation from within. Listening closely, she realized that the voices belonged to Baoyu and Baochai.
Daiyu grew angrier than ever. Turning it over and over in her mind, she suddenly remembered what had happened that morning: “Baoyu must be angry because I threatened to tell on him.
But when did I ever tell on you? You could at least have asked before becoming so angry with me that you treat me like this.
You refuse to let me in today, but do you imagine we shall never meet again tomorrow?”

The more she thought, the more heartsick she became. Heedless of the cold dew on the moss and the chill wind along the flower path, she stood alone beneath the blossoms by a corner of the wall and began to sob in bitter sorrow.

Daiyu possessed beauty unrivaled in her age and a grace rarely seen in the world. No sooner did she begin to weep than the roosting birds and crows among the nearby willow branches and blossoms, hearing her cries, all fluttered up and fled far away, unable to bear listening any longer.
Truly:
